Vector indexes introduce infrastructure and tuning requirements

name: Retrieval Reranking
description: Reranking applies a more expressive scoring model after initial retrieval to reorder candidate documents according to their relevance to a query.
limitations: Reranker errors can still affect final generation

name: Vector Database
description: A vector database or vector index stores embeddings and supports similarity search over large collections of represented objects.
advantages: Can combine vector similarity with metadata filters
limitations: Index configuration affects recall and latency
Vector similarity is not equivalent to semantic correctness

name: Hybrid Retrieval
description: Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic retrieval methods to exploit both exact term matching and semantic similarity.
advantages: Handles exact names and identifiers well
Often improves robustness across heterogeneous corpora

name: Context Compression
description: Context compression reduces a large retrieved or conversational context into a smaller representation while attempting to preserve information relevant to the current task.

name: Lost in the Middle
description: Lost-in-the-middle describes a tendency for language models to use information near the beginning or end of long contexts more effectively than information positioned in the middle.
implications: Context length alone is an insufficient measure of memory capability
Retrieval systems should consider context placement

sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

name: Needle-in-a-Haystack Evaluation
description: Needle-in-a-haystack evaluations place a specific piece of information inside increasingly large contexts and test whether the model can retrieve it.
limitations: Synthetic retrieval is not equivalent to real long-document reasoning
Success on one needle does not establish general long-context competence

name: Agent Memory
description: Agent memory systems provide persistent information storage and retrieval across multiple interactions or tasks.
advantages: Allows information to survive across sessions
limitations: Retrieval errors can compound over time
Memory management and forgetting are difficult

name: Retrieval Grounding
description: Retrieval grounding conditions generation on externally retrieved evidence with the goal of improving factual support and traceability.
advantages: Can improve factuality for knowledge-intensive tasks
limitations: Retrieved evidence can itself be wrong
Correct retrieval does not guarantee grounded generation

name: Retrieval Failure Modes
description: Retrieval systems can fail through missed relevant documents, irrelevant retrieval, incorrect ranking, insufficient context, duplicate results, or poor query formulation.

name: Parametric Memory vs Context vs Retrieval
description: Foundation-model systems can store or access information through learned parameters, temporary context, or external retrieval. These mechanisms have different update costs, capacities, and reliability characteristics.

name: Multimodal Foundation Model
description: A multimodal foundation model processes information from multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, video, or other signals within a shared or coordinated modeling system.
limitations: Performance can vary substantially across modalities

name: Vision-Language Model
description: A vision-language model combines visual and textual information to perform tasks such as image understanding, visual question answering, captioning, document analysis, and multimodal reasoning.

name: Vision Encoder
description: A vision encoder transforms an image or video frame into representations that can be consumed by a multimodal model.
advantages: Separates visual representation learning from language modeling
Allows pretrained vision models to be reused
limitations: Information may be lost during compression
Encoder choice strongly affects downstream capabilities

name: CLIP
description: CLIP learns aligned image and text representations through contrastive learning on large collections of image-text pairs.
limitations: Primarily a representation model rather than a general multimodal generator
Training data can contain web-scale biases

sources.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision

name: SigLIP
description: SigLIP is a vision-language representation model that uses a sigmoid-based image-text matching objective rather than the softmax contrastive formulation used by CLIP.
advantages: Useful as a vision encoder for multimodal systems
limitations: Downstream multimodal capabilities depend on integration with a language model

sources.title: Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training

name: Multimodal Projector
description: A multimodal projector maps representations produced by a modality-specific encoder into the representation space expected by another model, commonly a language model.
advantages: Allows pretrained encoders and language models to be combined
limitations: Projection quality depends on alignment training
Simple projectors may struggle with complex modality interactions

name: Cross-Attention Multimodal Fusion
description: Cross-attention allows representations from one modality to selectively attend to representations from another modality.
examples: video queries attending to frame representations
limitations: Repeated cross-attention can be expensive for long sequences

name: Flamingo
description: Flamingo is a multimodal model architecture that connects visual encoders with a language model using learned resampling and gated cross-attention mechanisms.
importance: Demonstrated powerful few-shot multimodal learning
Established an influential modular multimodal architecture

sources.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning

name: BLIP
description: BLIP combines vision-language understanding and generation through a unified architecture and bootstrapped image-caption data.

sources.title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation

name: BLIP-2
description: BLIP-2 connects a frozen image encoder to a frozen large language model through a lightweight Querying Transformer.
advantages: Efficiently connects pretrained vision and language models
Reduces the number of trainable parameters
limitations: Information must pass through the Q-Former bottleneck
Capabilities depend on the pretrained components

sources.title: BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models

name: LLaVA
description: LLaVA connects a pretrained vision encoder to a language model through a projection layer and trains the resulting system for visual instruction following.
limitations: Vision encoder limitations propagate to the model
Original design is primarily image-text rather than fully unified multimodal generation

name: Q-Former
description: Q-Former is a lightweight Transformer component that uses learned query representations to extract relevant information from frozen visual features before passing it to a language model.
limitations: Connector capacity limits the information transferred

sources.title: BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models

name: Perceiver Resampler
description: A Perceiver-style resampler converts a potentially large collection of modality-specific features into a smaller fixed-size set of latent representations.
advantages: Reduces computational burden for downstream language models
limitations: Latent count affects quality and efficiency

sources.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning

name: PaliGemma
description: PaliGemma combines a pretrained vision encoder with a Gemma language model to support vision-language tasks through a compact multimodal architecture.

name: Video-Language Model
description: Video-language models jointly process visual information across time and language to support video understanding, temporal reasoning, captioning, and video question answering.

name: Audio-Language Model
description: Audio-language models combine acoustic representations with language modeling to understand speech, environmental sounds, music, or other audio signals.

name: Multimodal Tokenization
description: Multimodal tokenization converts heterogeneous modalities into discrete or continuous representations that can be processed jointly by a multimodal model.
advantages: Provides a common interface for multimodal modeling
limitations: Token count can explode for high-resolution or long-duration modalities
Different modalities have fundamentally different statistical structures

name: Interleaved Multimodal Sequences
description: Interleaved multimodal architectures process sequences containing alternating or mixed modality elements such as text, images, audio, and video.
advantages: Supports richer document and web-like inputs
Allows relationships between multiple modalities within one context

name: Unified Multimodal Model
description: A unified multimodal model processes multiple modalities within a common modeling framework rather than treating each modality as an isolated external attachment to a language model.

name: Multimodal Alignment
description: Multimodal alignment trains representations from different modalities so that semantically related information can be associated and jointly reasoned over.
advantages: Allows pretrained modality-specific models to work together
limitations: Weak alignment can create modality grounding errors
Semantic equivalence is difficult to define

name: Multimodal Instruction Tuning
description: Multimodal instruction tuning adapts a multimodal model using instructions paired with inputs and desired responses involving one or more modalities.
advantages: Improves usability of multimodal foundation models
Connects multimodal perception with instruction following
limitations: Synthetic multimodal data can contain errors
Narrow datasets can produce modality-specific weaknesses

description: Multimodal hallucination occurs when a model generates content that is inconsistent with, unsupported by, or absent from the provided non-textual input.

name: Multimodal Grounding
description: Multimodal grounding measures or enables correspondence between model outputs and specific evidence contained in visual, auditory, textual, or other input modalities.
importance: Separates fluent generation from evidence-supported generation
Provides a basis for evaluating multimodal reliability
limitations: A model may identify evidence without faithfully using it
Localization does not automatically imply reasoning correctness

name: Tokenization
description: Tokenization converts raw input text or other modalities into units that a model can process as discrete tokens or structured representations.

name: Byte Pair Encoding
description: Byte Pair Encoding constructs a subword vocabulary by iteratively merging frequent symbol or token pairs.
mechanism: repeat until vocabulary target is reached
advantages: Balances vocabulary size and sequence length
Handles rare words through subword decomposition
limitations: Token boundaries can be linguistically arbitrary
Tokenizer behavior can affect downstream model performance

name: Byte-Level BPE
description: Byte-Level BPE performs subword tokenization over byte representations, allowing arbitrary text to be represented without requiring a fixed character vocabulary.
advantages: Avoids unknown characters in many settings
limitations: Token boundaries are not necessarily linguistically meaningful

name: WordPiece
description: WordPiece is a subword tokenization method that constructs a vocabulary designed to efficiently represent text while balancing vocabulary size and sequence length.
advantages: Widely used in encoder language models
limitations: Tokenization can vary significantly across languages
Subword boundaries are not equivalent to linguistic morphemes

name: SentencePiece
description: SentencePiece is a tokenizer framework that trains subword segmentation models directly from raw text without requiring language-specific whitespace preprocessing.
advantages: Does not require language-specific tokenization rules
limitations: Token efficiency depends on the trained vocabulary
Different languages can receive substantially different tokenization efficiency

name: Unigram Language Model Tokenization
description: Unigram tokenization models text as sequences of subword units and selects segmentations according to learned probabilities.
advantages: Useful for multilingual and diverse text
limitations: Segmentation behavior depends on the learned vocabulary

name: Multilingual Tokenization
description: Multilingual tokenization determines how a shared tokenizer represents text across languages, scripts, writing systems, and linguistic structures.

name: Token Fertility
description: Token fertility measures how many tokens are required to represent a given unit of text, such as a word, character sequence, or semantic content.
importance: Provides a practical measure of tokenizer efficiency
Affects context utilization
Affects inference and training cost
Useful for multilingual comparisons
limitations: Lower token count does not automatically imply better representations
Tokenization quality is language- and task-dependent

name: Tokenizer-Free Model
description: Tokenizer-free models process text directly at the byte or character level rather than relying on a conventional subword tokenizer.
advantages: Can simplify multilingual and unusual-text handling
Eliminates tokenizer mismatch between languages or domains
limitations: Sequence lengths can become substantially longer
Requires efficient architectures to process fine-grained inputs
Training and inference efficiency can be challenging

name: ByT5
description: ByT5 is a byte-level sequence-to-sequence Transformer that operates directly on UTF-8 bytes rather than using a conventional subword tokenizer.

architecture.tokenizer: none in the conventional subword sense

limitations: Higher computational cost without architectural efficiency techniques

sources.title: ByT5: Towards a Token-Free Future with Pre-trained Byte-to-Byte Models

name: CANINE
description: CANINE is a character-level Transformer architecture designed to process text without a conventional subword tokenizer while using downsampling and local processing to control sequence length.
advantages: Can improve robustness to spelling variation
limitations: Requires specialized architecture to manage sequence length

sources.title: CANINE: Pre-training an Efficient Tokenization-Free Encoder for Language Representation

name: Byte Latent Transformer
description: Byte Latent Transformer is a tokenizer-free architecture that operates on raw bytes while dynamically creating latent patches of bytes for more efficient computation.

architecture.design: compute allocated according to byte-level information

advantages: Addresses the sequence-length problem of raw-byte modeling
limitations: Architecture is more complex than conventional tokenized Transformers
Byte-level processing still requires efficient sequence compression

name: Embeddings
description: An embedding is a learned or constructed vector representation that maps discrete or structured inputs into a continuous numerical space.

name: Token Embeddings
description: Token embeddings map discrete token IDs to continuous vectors that form the initial representation of tokens entering a neural language model.
limitations: A token's initial embedding does not fully represent contextual meaning
Contextual representations are created by subsequent model layers

name: Contextual Representation
description: Contextual representations are token or sequence representations whose values depend on surrounding input and the transformations performed by the model.
advantages: Represents different meanings of the same token in different contexts
Supports complex semantic and syntactic reasoning
limitations: Representations are distributed and difficult to interpret directly

name: Sentence Embeddings
description: Sentence embeddings represent complete sentences or short text passages as vectors intended to capture semantic information useful for similarity and retrieval.
limitations: Compression into a single vector can lose fine-grained information
Embedding similarity does not guarantee factual equivalence

name: Dense Representation
description: A dense representation stores information across many dimensions of a continuous vector, with most dimensions containing non-zero values.
advantages: Well suited to neural similarity learning
limitations: Individual dimensions are often difficult to interpret
Dense similarity can miss exact lexical constraints

name: Sparse Representation
description: A sparse representation contains many zero or inactive dimensions and concentrates information in a relatively small subset of features.
advantages: Interpretable feature activation in some systems
Can represent rare lexical features effectively
limitations: Often less compact for dense semantic information
Large sparse spaces require specialized indexing

name: Sparse Representation
description: A sparse representation contains many zero or inactive dimensions and concentrates information in a relatively small subset of features.
advantages: Interpretable feature activation in some systems
Can represent rare lexical features effectively
limitations: Often less compact for dense semantic information
Large sparse spaces require specialized indexing

name: Learned Positional Embeddings
description: Learned positional embeddings assign trainable vectors to sequence positions so that Transformer models can distinguish token order.
limitations: Often tied to a fixed maximum position range
Extrapolation to longer contexts can be difficult

name: Absolute vs Relative Position Representation
description: Positional representations can encode absolute sequence positions directly or represent relative relationships between positions.

name: Tokenizer-Induced Bias
description: Tokenizer-induced bias occurs when tokenization choices systematically affect the computational cost, representation quality, or model behavior for particular languages, scripts, domains, or text patterns.

name: Tokens vs Semantic Units
description: A model token is a computational unit and does not necessarily correspond to a word, morpheme, concept, or semantic unit.
importance: Prevents misleading interpretation of token counts
Clarifies why token statistics differ across languages
Separates computational representation from linguistic structure

name: Tokens vs Semantic Units
description: A model token is a computational unit and does not necessarily correspond to a word, morpheme, concept, or semantic unit.
importance: Prevents misleading interpretation of token counts
Clarifies why token statistics differ across languages
Separates computational representation from linguistic structure

name: Foundation Model Evaluation
description: Foundation model evaluation measures capabilities, limitations, robustness, reliability, efficiency, and safety across standardized or task-specific tests.
limitations: Benchmark scores are incomplete measurements of capability
Models can overfit to benchmark formats
Different prompting and evaluation protocols can change results

name: Benchmark
description: A benchmark is a standardized evaluation dataset, task, protocol, or suite designed to compare model performance on a defined capability or problem class.
limitations: A benchmark measures only the capability encoded by its design
Leaderboard rankings may depend on evaluation details

name: MMLU
description: Massive Multitask Language Understanding evaluates models across a broad collection of academic and professional subjects using multiple-choice questions.
importance: Became a widely used general-purpose language-model benchmark
Provides broad subject coverage
limitations: Multiple-choice format does not represent all real-world reasoning
Performance can approach saturation for newer models

name: MMLU-Pro
description: MMLU-Pro is an enhanced evaluation designed to provide more challenging and reasoning-oriented questions than the original MMLU.
limitations: Still represents a constrained benchmark format
Does not establish broad real-world competence

name: GPQA
description: Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A evaluates advanced scientific reasoning using difficult questions written by domain experts.
importance: Targets difficult questions intended to resist straightforward web lookup
Useful for evaluating advanced scientific reasoning
limitations: Results can depend on evaluation prompting

sources.title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark

name: GSM8K
description: GSM8K evaluates multi-step mathematical reasoning using grade-school word problems.
importance: Became a widely used mathematical reasoning benchmark for language models
limitations: Modern reasoning models can saturate the benchmark
Does not represent advanced mathematical reasoning

sources.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems

name: MATH
description: The MATH benchmark evaluates mathematical problem solving across competition-style mathematics problems with varying difficulty.

sources.title: Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset

name: HumanEval
description: HumanEval evaluates code-generation models on programming problems using functional correctness tests.
importance: Established functional testing as an important method for evaluating code generation
limitations: Limited representation of real software engineering

sources.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code

name: SWE-bench
description: SWE-bench evaluates models on real-world software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub repositories, including issue resolution and code changes.
importance: Moves code evaluation beyond isolated programming problems
Tests interaction with real repositories and software engineering workflows
limitations: Patch success does not capture every aspect of engineering quality

sources.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?

name: HumanEval+
description: HumanEval+ expands the HumanEval test suite with additional automatically generated tests to provide stronger functional correctness evaluation.

name: MMMU
description: MMMU evaluates multimodal reasoning using university-level questions that require understanding both visual and textual information.

name: BIG-bench
description: BIG-bench is a broad collaborative benchmark containing hundreds of tasks designed to probe diverse capabilities and limitations of language models.
importance: Provides broad task diversity
Useful for studying emergent and unusual capabilities
limitations: Large task diversity makes aggregate interpretation difficult
Individual tasks vary substantially in difficulty and relevance

sources.title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models

name: HellaSwag
description: HellaSwag evaluates commonsense reasoning by asking models to select the most plausible continuation of a scenario.

name: AI2 Reasoning Challenge
description: The AI2 Reasoning Challenge evaluates science-question answering with a focus on reasoning beyond simple retrieval.

name: TruthfulQA
description: TruthfulQA evaluates whether models produce truthful responses to questions designed to trigger common misconceptions and false beliefs.
importance: Highlights the distinction between plausible language generation and truthful responses
limitations: Truthfulness is difficult to capture with a single benchmark
Evaluation judgments can depend on answer interpretation

name: LongBench
description: LongBench evaluates long-context language-model performance across multiple tasks and domains rather than relying only on synthetic context retrieval.
importance: Tests practical long-context use
Provides broader evaluation than a single needle-in-a-haystack test
limitations: Long-context capability remains difficult to summarize with one score

name: RULER
description: RULER evaluates long-context capabilities using controlled synthetic tasks designed to probe retrieval and reasoning at different context lengths.
advantages: Provides controlled evaluation across context lengths
Can expose degradation hidden by advertised context windows
limitations: Synthetic tasks do not fully represent real-world long documents

name: Benchmark Contamination
description: Benchmark contamination occurs when evaluation examples or information derived from them appear in a model's training data, potentially inflating measured performance.

name: Benchmark Saturation
description: Benchmark saturation occurs when many capable models achieve near-ceiling performance, reducing the benchmark's ability to distinguish between them.
effects: greater importance of minor protocol differences

name: Evaluation Protocol
description: An evaluation protocol defines how a model is prompted, sampled, scored, constrained, and compared during a benchmark evaluation.
importance: The same model can produce different scores under different protocols
Reproducibility requires protocol transparency

name: Human Evaluation
description: Human evaluation uses human judgments to assess qualities that are difficult to capture reliably with automated metrics.

name: LLM-as-a-Judge
description: LLM-as-a-Judge uses a language model to evaluate or compare outputs generated by other models.
advantages: Lower cost than large-scale human evaluation

name: Model Calibration
description: Calibration measures whether a model's confidence corresponds appropriately to the probability that its predictions are correct.
importance: Separates confidence from correctness
Important for high-stakes decision systems
limitations: Calibration can vary by task and distribution
Language-model confidence is difficult to interpret directly

name: Robustness Evaluation
description: Robustness evaluation measures whether model behavior remains reliable when inputs, wording, domains, distributions, or environmental conditions change.
importance: Measures stability outside ideal benchmark conditions
limitations: No finite test suite can cover all possible shifts

name: Adversarial Evaluation
description: Adversarial evaluation intentionally constructs difficult or malicious inputs to discover model weaknesses, unsafe behavior, or reliability failures.
advantages: Finds failure modes that ordinary benchmarks may miss
Useful for safety testing and red teaming
limitations: Success against one attack does not establish universal robustness

name: Real-World Task Evaluation
description: Real-world evaluation measures model performance within realistic workflows, environments, tools, constraints, and user objectives rather than isolated benchmark questions.
limitations: Results depend heavily on environment design

name: Benchmark Overfitting
description: Benchmark overfitting occurs when model development or prompt engineering becomes excessively optimized for known evaluation sets rather than general capability.

name: Benchmark Suite
description: A benchmark suite combines multiple evaluations to measure different capabilities rather than reducing model quality to a single task or score.
limitations: Aggregate scores can hide important weaknesses
Different benchmarks may have different contamination and difficulty levels

name: Benchmark Score vs Actual Capability
description: Benchmark performance is evidence about a specific tested capability, not a complete measurement of a model's general intelligence, reliability, or real-world usefulness.
principle: A benchmark score should be interpreted together with its task definition, evaluation protocol, contamination risk, and deployment context.

name: Foundation Model Training Data
description: Training data is the collection of text, code, images, audio, video, or other information used to develop a foundation model.
importance: Training data strongly influences model capabilities
Data composition affects specialization and generalization
Data quality can matter as much as raw dataset size
limitations: Exact training datasets are often only partially disclosed
Web-scale data can contain duplication, misinformation, copyrighted material, and harmful content
Dataset composition can be difficult to independently verify

name: Pretraining
description: Pretraining is the large-scale learning stage in which a foundation model learns general representations or predictive capabilities from broad datasets before task-specific adaptation.
advantages: Allows later adaptation to many tasks
limitations: Training data may contain unwanted biases or sensitive information

name: Next-Token Prediction
description: Next-token prediction trains an autoregressive language model to predict the next token given the preceding sequence.
objective: maximize the probability of the next token conditioned on previous tokens
advantages: Uses naturally occurring text without task labels
limitations: The objective does not directly specify factuality, reasoning, or helpfulness
Training distribution determines what the model learns to predict

name: Masked Language Modeling
description: Masked language modeling trains a model to reconstruct tokens that have been hidden or corrupted within an input sequence.
limitations: Training corruption may differ from downstream tasks
Not naturally identical to autoregressive generation

name: Denoising Objective
description: Denoising objectives train models to reconstruct clean sequences or representations from corrupted inputs.

name: Training Data Mixture
description: A training data mixture defines the relative composition and sampling proportions of different datasets, domains, languages, modalities, or quality levels used during training.
importance: Different mixtures can produce different capability profiles
Small high-quality subsets can receive disproportionate sampling weight
limitations: Reported dataset percentages may not reveal actual training exposure

name: Data Curation
description: Data curation is the process of selecting, cleaning, filtering, transforming, deduplicating, and organizing data before or during model training.

name: Data Quality Filtering
description: Quality filtering attempts to remove low-value, noisy, malformed, irrelevant, or otherwise undesirable examples from large training corpora.
advantages: Can increase the proportion of useful examples
limitations: Filters can remove useful but unusual data

name: Data Deduplication
description: Data deduplication identifies and removes duplicate or near-duplicate examples from training corpora.
limitations: Aggressive deduplication can remove legitimate repeated information
Near-duplicate detection can be computationally expensive

name: Common Crawl
description: Common Crawl is a large open repository of web crawl data that has been used as a source for numerous research and language-model training datasets.
importance: Major source of web-scale text
Foundation for many derived language-model datasets
limitations: May contain duplicated, low-quality, copyrighted, or harmful content

name: C4
description: C4 is a large cleaned web corpus derived from Common Crawl and designed for language-model pretraining.
importance: Used in the development of T5 and related research
Influential example of large-scale web-data curation
limitations: Filtering rules can introduce dataset biases
Web content remains noisy and heterogeneous

name: RefinedWeb
description: RefinedWeb is a large-scale web dataset produced through extensive filtering and deduplication of Common Crawl data.
importance: Demonstrated that heavily curated web data can support strong language-model training
Associated with the Falcon model family
limitations: Exact representation of the entire web is not guaranteed

name: RedPajama
description: RedPajama is an open effort to reproduce and provide components of large-scale language-model training datasets and pipelines.
importance: Expanded open access to large-scale pretraining data
Supported reproducible language-model research

name: Dolma
description: Dolma is an open corpus designed for language-model pretraining, combining multiple data sources with documented processing and filtering pipelines.
importance: Supports open foundation-model research
Provides greater transparency into data construction than many proprietary datasets

name: FineWeb
description: FineWeb is a large-scale dataset derived from Common Crawl using extensive filtering and deduplication intended to produce high-quality web text for language-model pretraining.
importance: Provides an openly documented large-scale web corpus
Useful for studying the effect of web-data quality on language-model training

name: The Stack
description: The Stack is a large collection of source code intended to support research on code models, with filtering and opt-out mechanisms designed to address data governance concerns.
limitations: Code licensing and provenance require careful handling
Repositories can contain duplicated or low-quality code

name: Synthetic Training Data
description: Synthetic training data is generated by models or procedural systems and subsequently used to train or improve another model.
advantages: Can produce large quantities of targeted examples
Can reduce dependence on manually authored data

name: Training Data Contamination
description: Training data contamination occurs when evaluation material, benchmark examples, test data, or protected information becomes part of a model's training corpus.

name: Training Data Memorization
description: Training data memorization occurs when a model retains and can reproduce specific information or sequences encountered during training.

name: Data Weighting
description: Data weighting changes how frequently different datasets, domains, languages, or examples are sampled during training.

name: Curriculum Learning
description: Curriculum learning controls the order or difficulty distribution of training examples rather than sampling all examples uniformly throughout training.
advantages: Can control exposure to different data types
limitations: Optimal curriculum is model- and dataset-dependent

name: Instruction-Tuning Data
description: Instruction-tuning data consists of examples pairing instructions or user requests with desired model responses.

name: Preference Data
description: Preference data contains comparisons or judgments indicating which of multiple model outputs is preferred according to human or automated evaluators.
limitations: Human judgments may encode evaluator biases

name: Data Quality vs Data Scale
description: Foundation-model training depends on both dataset scale and dataset quality. Increasing raw data volume does not necessarily produce proportional capability improvements.
principle: More data is not automatically better data.

name: Training Data Governance
description: Training data governance concerns provenance, licensing, privacy, consent, documentation, filtering, access controls, and responsible use of data in model development.
importance: Training data decisions affect legal and ethical risk
Documentation improves reproducibility and accountability

name: Post-Training
description: Post-training is the set of optimization stages applied after large-scale pretraining to improve instruction following, task performance, preference alignment, reasoning, safety, and practical usability.

name: Supervised Fine-Tuning
description: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using curated examples containing inputs, instructions, and desired outputs.
advantages: Works with relatively small datasets compared with pretraining
limitations: Can narrow model behavior if data diversity is limited
Does not directly optimize relative preferences

name: Instruction Tuning
description: Instruction tuning trains a pretrained model on diverse task instructions and corresponding responses so that it can generalize instruction-following behavior across tasks.

name: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
description: RLHF uses human preference judgments to train a reward model and then optimize the language model toward responses that receive higher predicted reward.
advantages: Supports behavioral objectives that are difficult to specify as supervised labels

name: Reward Model
description: A reward model learns to assign a scalar preference score to model outputs based on preference judgments.

name: Proximal Policy Optimization
description: Proximal Policy Optimization is a policy-gradient reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to make policy updates more stable by constraining the magnitude of changes between successive policies.
limitations: Sensitive to reward-model quality and hyperparameters

name: Direct Preference Optimization
description: Direct Preference Optimization trains a language model directly from preference pairs without requiring a separately optimized reward model and reinforcement-learning loop in the standard formulation.
advantages: Simpler training pipeline than traditional RLHF
limitations: Reference-model and objective choices affect behavior

sources.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

name: Identity Preference Optimization
description: Identity Preference Optimization is a preference-learning approach related to direct preference optimization that modifies the preference objective to address potential issues in preference-model optimization.

name: Kahneman-Tversky Optimization
description: Kahneman-Tversky Optimization is a preference-learning approach designed to work with desirable and undesirable responses without requiring traditional pairwise preference data in the same form as DPO.
advantages: Can work with unpaired preference signals
Provides an alternative to pairwise preference optimization
limitations: Alternative objectives introduce their own optimization assumptions

name: Rejection Sampling
description: Rejection sampling generates multiple candidate outputs and retains examples that satisfy a quality criterion, verifier, reward model, or preference signal.
advantages: Can convert model-generated outputs into training data
limitations: Quality depends on the scoring mechanism
Generating many candidates can be computationally expensive

name: Knowledge Distillation
description: Knowledge distillation transfers useful behavior or representations from a teacher model into a student model.
limitations: Student quality depends on teacher quality

name: Constitutional AI
description: Constitutional AI is an alignment methodology that uses explicit principles or a constitution to guide model critique, revision, and preference optimization.
advantages: Reduces reliance on direct human labeling for every example
limitations: Quality depends on the chosen principles
Automated feedback can reproduce model biases

name: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
description: RLAIF uses AI-generated evaluations or preferences as feedback for reinforcement-learning or preference-optimization pipelines.
advantages: Can reduce dependence on large quantities of human preference labels

name: Process Supervision
description: Process supervision provides feedback on intermediate reasoning steps rather than evaluating only the final answer.
advantages: Can identify errors before the final answer
limitations: A locally correct step sequence does not guarantee global correctness

name: Outcome Supervision
description: Outcome supervision evaluates whether the final answer or task result is correct without directly supervising every intermediate reasoning step.
advantages: Applicable to many tasks with automatically verifiable outcomes
limitations: Can reward incorrect intermediate reasoning that happens to reach the correct answer

name: Process Reward Model
description: A process reward model evaluates intermediate reasoning steps and provides feedback about the quality or correctness of a reasoning trajectory.
advantages: Can help distinguish partially correct from incorrect reasoning trajectories
limitations: Evaluating reasoning steps can itself be difficult

name: Verifier
description: A verifier evaluates whether a generated solution, reasoning trajectory, program, proof, or final answer satisfies a correctness criterion.
advantages: Allows multiple candidate solutions to be compared
limitations: Incorrect verification can reinforce incorrect solutions

name: Best-of-N Sampling
description: Best-of-N sampling generates multiple candidate solutions and selects the candidate receiving the highest score from a verifier, reward model, or evaluation function.
advantages: Can improve performance without changing model weights
Uses additional inference compute to search solution space

name: Self-Consistency
description: Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and selects an answer based on agreement among the generated solutions.
advantages: Can improve reasoning accuracy without parameter updates

name: Test-Time Compute
description: Test-time compute increases the amount of computation or search performed during inference in order to improve the quality of generated solutions.
importance: Introduces a second axis of scaling beyond model parameter count
Can trade additional inference compute for improved task performance

name: Reasoning Model
description: A reasoning model is a model explicitly trained, optimized, or deployed to allocate additional computation or structured generation toward difficult reasoning tasks.
limitations: Reasoning traces do not necessarily guarantee factual correctness

name: Reasoning-Oriented Training
description: Reasoning-oriented training increases a model's ability to solve multi-step problems through supervised reasoning examples, reinforcement learning, verification, synthetic data, or combinations of these methods.

name: Reward Hacking
description: Reward hacking occurs when a model discovers behaviors that increase the measured reward without actually achieving the intended objective.

name: Specification Gaming
description: Specification gaming occurs when a system satisfies the literal or measurable specification of an objective while violating the intended goal.
principle: Optimizing the metric is not always equivalent to achieving the intended objective.

name: Scaling Laws
description: Scaling laws describe empirical relationships between model performance, model size, dataset size, and computational budget.
principle: Model performance often improves predictably as relevant scale dimensions increase, although the relationship depends on architecture, data quality, objective, and evaluation task.
importance: Guides training-budget decisions
Helps estimate returns from additional compute
Provides a framework for comparing model size and dataset size
limitations: Scaling relationships are empirical rather than universal laws
Data quality and architecture can change scaling behavior

name: Kaplan Scaling Laws
description: Kaplan et al. studied empirical scaling relationships between language-model loss and model size, dataset size, and compute.
importance: Established an influential framework for predicting language-model scaling behavior
Helped motivate larger model and compute investments
limitations: Later work revised conclusions about compute-optimal allocation
Results depend on training regime and assumptions

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

name: Chinchilla Scaling
description: Chinchilla scaling describes compute-optimal training results suggesting that many large language models were undertrained relative to their parameter count and that additional training data can be highly valuable.
principle: For a fixed compute budget, model size and training-token count should be balanced rather than allocating nearly all scaling to parameters.
importance: Changed how researchers think about parameter count versus training data
Motivated smaller models trained on substantially more tokens
limitations: Optimal ratios depend on architecture, data quality, optimizer, and training regime
The original conclusions concern training compute rather than every deployment scenario

name: Compute-Optimal Training
description: Compute-optimal training attempts to maximize model quality for a fixed computational budget by jointly choosing model size, training data, and training duration.
objective: maximize capability or minimize loss for a fixed compute budget

name: Training Compute
description: Training compute represents the computational work required to optimize a model over its training data.

name: FLOPs
description: FLOPs, or floating-point operations, provide a measure of the number of arithmetic operations performed during model training or inference.
caution: FLOPs measure computational work but do not directly equal wall-clock time, monetary cost, or energy consumption.

name: Parameter Count
description: Parameter count measures the number of learned numerical parameters in a model.
caution: Parameter count alone does not determine capability, training compute, inference cost, or active computation in sparse models.

name: Active Parameters
description: Active parameters are the subset of model parameters actually used for a particular input during a forward pass, especially relevant to mixture-of-experts architectures.
importance: Distinguishes total model capacity from per-token computation
Useful for understanding sparse model efficiency

name: Inference Compute
description: Inference compute is the computational work required to produce model outputs after training.

name: Inference Cost
description: Inference cost represents the economic resources required to serve model requests at deployment time.

name: Inference Latency
description: Inference latency measures the time required to process a request or generate a model response.

name: Inference Throughput
description: Inference throughput measures how many tokens, requests, or tasks a serving system can process over a unit of time.

name: Mixture-of-Experts Efficiency
description: Mixture-of-Experts architectures increase total parameter capacity while activating only a subset of experts for each input.
advantages: Lower per-token computation than an equivalently sized dense model

name: Expert Routing
description: Expert routing determines which specialized neural-network experts process each token or input in a mixture-of-experts model.

name: Load-Balancing Loss
description: Load-balancing losses encourage mixture-of-experts routers to distribute tokens across experts rather than concentrating computation on a small subset.

name: Quantization
description: Quantization represents model weights, activations, or caches using lower-precision numerical formats to reduce memory usage and computational cost.

name: Weight-Only Quantization
description: Weight-only quantization reduces the numerical precision of model parameters while leaving activations at a higher precision.
limitations: Accuracy depends on quantization method and model architecture

name: GPTQ
description: GPTQ is a post-training weight-quantization method designed to compress large language models to low precision while attempting to preserve model quality.

name: AWQ
description: Activation-aware Weight Quantization is a low-bit weight-quantization method that uses activation information to identify weights that are especially important to preserve.
advantages: Designed around activation-aware protection of important weights
limitations: Performance depends on hardware and implementation

name: Mixed-Precision Computing
description: Mixed-precision computing uses different numerical precisions for different operations, tensors, or training stages.

name: Model Pruning
description: Pruning removes parameters, neurons, attention structures, or other computational components judged to be unnecessary.
advantages: Can reduce computation when supported by hardware
limitations: Unstructured sparsity may not produce practical speedups
Aggressive pruning can reduce model quality

name: Model Sparsity
description: Sparsity represents computational or parameter structures in which only a subset of values or components are active.
advantages: Potential reduction in computation and memory
limitations: Speedups require hardware and software support

name: Distillation for Efficiency
description: Distillation transfers useful behavior from a larger teacher model into a smaller student model to reduce deployment cost while retaining selected capabilities.

name: Speculative Decoding
description: Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose multiple tokens that are then verified by a larger target model, potentially increasing generation throughput without changing the target model's output distribution under the standard exact formulation.
advantages: Does not require changing target-model weights

name: FlashAttention
description: FlashAttention is an exact attention algorithm that improves GPU memory efficiency and speed by organizing computation and memory access to reduce expensive reads and writes to high-bandwidth memory.
advantages: Enables longer sequences under constrained memory
limitations: Benefits depend on hardware and implementation
Primarily addresses attention computation rather than the entire model

name: KV Cache
description: A key-value cache stores attention keys and values from previously processed tokens so autoregressive decoding does not repeatedly recompute them.
benefit: reduces redundant computation during autoregressive generation
cost: KV cache memory grows with sequence length, layers, attention heads, and batch size
importance: Critical for long-context inference
Can become a major memory bottleneck in serving systems

name: Paged Attention
description: Paged attention manages key-value cache memory using block-based allocation inspired by virtual memory systems.
advantages: Supports dynamic batching and variable-length requests

name: Continuous Batching
description: Continuous batching dynamically adds and removes requests from a running inference batch rather than waiting for an entire static batch to finish.
advantages: Better handling of variable generation lengths

name: Memory Bandwidth Bottleneck
description: Memory bandwidth can limit model throughput when computation spends significant time moving weights, activations, or cache data rather than performing arithmetic.
importance: Explains why theoretical FLOPs alone do not predict serving speed
Motivates quantization and memory-efficient kernels

name: Compute vs Memory Bottlenecks
description: Model performance can be limited either by arithmetic computation or by memory movement, depending on the workload, hardware, model architecture, and inference stage.
importance: Explains why algorithmic FLOP reductions do not always produce proportional speedups

name: Energy Efficiency
description: Energy efficiency measures the computational or task performance achieved per unit of energy consumed.

name: Context Window
description: The context window is the amount of input and generated-token context that a model can process within a single inference sequence.
importance: Determines how much information can be presented to the model at once
Affects long-document processing
Affects KV-cache memory and inference cost
limitations: A larger context window does not guarantee effective use of all information
Longer contexts increase computational or memory requirements
Information can be lost or underutilized within very long contexts

name: Long-Context Modeling
description: Long-context modeling enables foundation models to process substantially longer sequences than conventional language models.

name: Positional Encoding
description: Positional encoding provides information about token order because standard self-attention does not inherently encode sequence position.

name: Rotary Position Embedding
description: Rotary Position Embedding encodes token positions by applying position-dependent rotations to query and key representations.
advantages: Naturally integrates position information into attention
Widely adopted in modern language models
limitations: Original configuration has limitations when extrapolated far beyond training context
Long-context extension often requires additional scaling techniques

name: RoPE Scaling
description: RoPE scaling modifies the frequency structure of rotary positional embeddings to extend the usable context length of models.
advantages: Can extend context without retraining an entirely new model from scratch
limitations: Very long extrapolation can degrade positional resolution
Effectiveness depends on model architecture and adaptation method

name: ALiBi
description: Attention with Linear Biases adds position-dependent linear biases directly to attention scores instead of using explicit positional embeddings.
advantages: Can provide useful length generalization properties
limitations: Not universally superior to rotary or other positional methods

name: Position Interpolation
description: Position interpolation extends a model's usable context by mapping positions from a longer target sequence into the positional range encountered during training.
advantages: Can extend context with relatively efficient adaptation
limitations: Very large extensions may require additional training or specialized techniques

name: Attention Dilution
description: Attention dilution refers to the difficulty of reliably focusing on relevant information as the amount of contextual information increases.

name: Lost in the Middle
description: Lost-in-the-middle describes a tendency observed in some language models to use information near the beginning or end of a long context more reliably than information positioned in the middle.
importance: Shows that context-window size is not equivalent to effective information retrieval
Motivates dedicated long-context evaluation
limitations: Severity varies across models, tasks, prompts, and context lengths

name: External Memory
description: External memory systems provide models with information stored outside the model parameters and immediate context window.
advantages: Allows information to be updated without retraining model weights
Can provide access to private or domain-specific information
Can reduce dependence on memorized knowledge

name: Information Retrieval
description: Information retrieval is the process of finding relevant documents, passages, records, or other information from a collection in response to a query.

name: BM25
description: BM25 is a widely used lexical information-retrieval scoring function based primarily on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization.
limitations: May miss semantically related text expressed with different vocabulary

name: Dense Retrieval
description: Dense retrieval represents queries and documents as vectors and retrieves items based on vector similarity.
advantages: Can retrieve conceptually related text with limited lexical overlap

name: Hybrid Retrieval
description: Hybrid retrieval combines multiple retrieval mechanisms, commonly lexical and dense retrieval, to improve coverage across different query types.
advantages: Combines exact matching with semantic matching
limitations: Requires score fusion or ranking strategy

name: Reranking
description: Reranking applies a more expressive scoring model to an initial set of retrieved candidates in order to improve the ordering of the most relevant results.
advantages: Can improve relevance of top-ranked results
Allows inexpensive retrieval followed by expensive scoring on a smaller candidate set

name: Embedding Model
description: An embedding model maps text, images, audio, or other objects into numerical vector representations designed to capture useful semantic or structural relationships.

name: Vector Database
description: A vector database or vector index stores embeddings and supports similarity search over large collections of vector representations.

name: HNSW
description: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs provide an approximate nearest-neighbor indexing method for efficient similarity search in high-dimensional vector spaces.
advantages: Widely used in vector search systems

name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description: Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines information retrieval with generative modeling by supplying retrieved external information to a generator.
advantages: Provides access to external or current information
Can ground generation in retrieved sources

name: RAG Pipeline
description: A RAG pipeline connects document ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, reranking, context construction, and generation.

name: Document Chunking
description: Document chunking divides large documents into smaller retrieval units that can be embedded, indexed, retrieved, and supplied to a model.

name: Query Rewriting
description: Query rewriting transforms a user's original query into one or more retrieval-oriented queries intended to improve search coverage or relevance.
advantages: Useful for ambiguous or complex questions

name: Query Decomposition
description: Query decomposition breaks a complex question into smaller subqueries that can be independently retrieved or solved before combining the results.
advantages: Improves retrieval for questions requiring multiple sources
limitations: Incorrect decomposition can omit important information

name: Multi-Hop Retrieval
description: Multi-hop retrieval retrieves information through multiple connected retrieval steps when a question cannot be answered from a single passage or document.

name: Memory Compression
description: Memory compression reduces the amount of information that must remain explicitly represented while attempting to preserve information needed for future model computation.
limitations: Quality depends on what information is preserved

name: Recurrent Memory
description: Recurrent memory mechanisms maintain a compact state that is updated across segments or interactions, allowing models to process information beyond a single fixed context window.
advantages: Can reduce the need to attend over the entire historical sequence
limitations: Memory state management introduces additional architectural complexity

name: Context Caching
description: Context caching reuses previously computed representations for repeated or shared prefixes, reducing redundant inference computation.

name: Multimodal Foundation Model
description: A multimodal foundation model processes information from multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, video, or other structured inputs within a shared or coordinated modeling system.

name: Vision-Language Model
description: A vision-language model combines visual information with natural-language representations to perform tasks involving images and text.

name: Vision Encoder
description: A vision encoder transforms images or video frames into representations that can be consumed by a multimodal language model.

name: Multimodal Projector
description: A multimodal projector maps representations from a modality-specific encoder into the representation space expected by a language model.

name: Cross-Attention
description: Cross-attention allows representations from one modality or sequence to attend to representations from another source.
mechanism: keys and values from another representation

name: Multimodal Fusion
description: Multimodal fusion combines information from multiple modalities so that a model can jointly reason over their relationships.

name: Early Fusion
description: Early fusion combines modality representations near the beginning of the model's processing pipeline.

name: Late Fusion
description: Late fusion combines modality-specific predictions or representations after substantial independent processing.
advantages: Can simplify integration of independently trained components

name: Shared Multimodal Latent Space
description: A shared latent space represents information from multiple modalities in a common representation space where relationships between modalities can be learned.

name: CLIP
description: CLIP learns aligned image and text representations using contrastive learning over image-text pairs.
limitations: Primarily designed for representation alignment rather than general conversational generation

name: SigLIP
description: SigLIP is a vision-language representation model that replaces the traditional CLIP-style softmax contrastive loss with a sigmoid-based objective applied to image-text pairs.
advantages: Useful as a vision encoder for multimodal systems

name: Flamingo
description: Flamingo is a multimodal model architecture designed to process interleaved visual and textual inputs and perform few-shot multimodal tasks.

name: Perceiver Resampler
description: The Perceiver Resampler compresses variable-size visual representations into a fixed number of latent representations that can be consumed by a language model.

name: BLIP
description: BLIP is a vision-language pretraining framework combining understanding and generation objectives for image-text tasks.

name: BLIP-2
description: BLIP-2 connects a frozen image encoder with a frozen large language model through a lightweight Querying Transformer.

name: Q-Former
description: Q-Former is a lightweight transformer component that extracts task-relevant visual information from a frozen vision encoder for use by a language model.

name: LLaVA
description: LLaVA connects a pretrained vision encoder to a large language model through a learned projection layer and instruction-tunes the resulting multimodal system.

name: IDEFICS
description: IDEFICS is an open multimodal language model family designed for interleaved image-text understanding and generation.

name: PaliGemma
description: PaliGemma combines a vision encoder with a Gemma language model for image-and-text tasks.

name: Qwen-VL
description: Qwen-VL is a vision-language model family combining visual understanding with the Qwen language-model family.

name: Qwen2-VL
description: Qwen2-VL is a multimodal model family designed for image and video understanding with flexible visual input processing.

name: InternVL
description: InternVL is an open vision-language model family designed for high-resolution image understanding and multimodal reasoning.

name: Pixtral
description: Pixtral is a multimodal model family from Mistral designed to process images alongside text.

name: Molmo
description: Molmo is an open vision-language model family focused on strong multimodal understanding with publicly released model components and data resources.

name: KOSMOS
description: KOSMOS is a multimodal language-model family exploring unified processing of text, images, and other perceptual inputs.

name: Chameleon
description: Chameleon explores early-fusion multimodal modeling in which text and image representations can be integrated into a shared token sequence.
importance: Demonstrates an alternative to simply attaching a vision encoder to an existing language model
Explores unified multimodal token processing

name: Janus
description: Janus is a unified multimodal model family that separates visual understanding and visual generation representations while using a shared autoregressive language-modeling framework.

name: Unified Multimodal Model
description: A unified multimodal model uses a common modeling framework or representation system to process multiple modalities rather than treating every modality as an entirely separate pipeline.
limitations: Different modalities have very different information structures
Training and representation alignment are challenging

name: Visual Tokens
description: Visual tokens are discrete or continuous representations of image regions, patches, features, or latent visual information that can be processed by a multimodal model.

name: Video Understanding
description: Video understanding extends visual-language modeling to sequences of frames and temporal information.

name: Audio-Language Model
description: An audio-language model combines audio representations with language modeling to understand or generate information involving speech and other sounds.

name: Speech Encoder
description: A speech encoder transforms audio waveforms or acoustic features into representations that can be consumed by a language or multimodal model.

name: Multimodal Tokenization
description: Multimodal tokenization converts information from different modalities into representations that can be processed within a common or coordinated model.

name: Multimodal Reasoning
description: Multimodal reasoning requires combining information across modalities to derive an answer, plan, explanation, or decision.

name: BLIP-2
architecture: vision encoder plus Q-Former plus language model

name: InstructBLIP
architecture: vision encoder plus Q-Former plus language model

name: LLaVA
organization: University of Wisconsin–Madison / Microsoft Research / community

name: LLaVA-1.5
architecture: CLIP vision encoder plus language model

name: Flamingo
architecture: vision encoder plus language model with cross-attention

name: PaliGemma
architecture: SigLIP vision encoder plus Gemma language model
